flowering.short: Pollinated flowers drop; unpollinated blooms can turn wine-colored
flowering.guidance: University of Maryland Extension describes blueberry flowering generally: plump flower buds differ from slender leaf buds, and each flower bud produces several flowers. It notes that native bees are effective pollinators, unpollinated blooms turn wine-colored, and pollinated flowers drop after about 5–6 days. These are blueberry-level diagnostic cues, not a cultivar-specific bloom date or a guarantee of fruit set.
items: Distinguish plump flower buds from slender leaf buds.
A bloom changing wine-color can indicate it was not pollinated; a pollinated flower normally drops after several days.

maintenance.guidance: University of Maryland Extension describes renewal pruning: remove older, declining canes to encourage replacement growth. Young plants are managed differently from established bushes; do not apply mature-bush pruning immediately to a new transplant.
items: Allow young plants to establish before applying mature-bush pruning.

growth.short: Perennial roots produce canes with a two-year cycle in summer-bearing types
growth.guidance: The roots are perennial and canes are biennial. In summer-bearing red raspberries, first-year primocanes generally fruit as floricanes the next season and then die; many red raspberry cultivars also fruit on first-year primocanes. Penn State describes red raspberry suckers as arising primarily from roots, eventually forming a hedgerow or unmanaged patch. This record does not assign one bearing habit to an unspecified cultivar.
items: Identify whether the cultivar bears on second-year canes or first-year primocanes.

maintenance.short: Pruning depends on the fruiting type

items: Confirm the bearing type before selecting a pruning schedule.

Frequent picking helps avoid overripe fruit remaining on canes.

Diseased cane removal and airflow are source-backed sanitation measures; no disease resistance is asserted.
